 Dengue fever is difficult to predict, and a person can contract the disease multiple times.
 Dengue fever is now prevalent year-round, no longer following a distinct season as before. All four types of dengue virus coexist in Vietnam, increasing the risk of reinfection and severe illness.
 Báo Sài Gòn Giải phóng • 06/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 All four types of dengue fever virus are circulating in Vietnam. Photo: NGOC DUNG On November 6th, in Hanoi, the Department of Disease Prevention ( Ministry of Health ) organized the Dengue Fever Conference 2026, with the participation of over 700 domestic and international delegates. At the conference, Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention, stated that in the first 10 months of 2026, the whole country recorded over 170,600 cases of dengue fever and 21 deaths. The number of cases increased by 26% compared to the same period in 2025. The South accounted for 66.8% of the total cases, the Central Highlands 17.5%, the Central region 9.8%, and the North 5.9%.
 According to Mr. Hoang Minh Duc, despite the implementation of numerous disease prevention and control measures, dengue fever is still prevalent in Vietnam. Given the increasingly unpredictable nature of the disease, the health sector is reviewing and evaluating the effectiveness of existing solutions, updating scientific advancements, and seeking more proactive and appropriate preventive measures. 
 Dr. Hoang Minh Duc, Director of the Department of Disease Prevention (Ministry of Health), spoke at the conference. Analyzing the disease's progression, Professor Nguyen Van Kinh, former Director of the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases, stated that after the outbreak in 2022, the number of dengue fever cases continued to increase. Notably, the disease no longer follows a clear seasonal or cyclical pattern as before. Currently, all four dengue virus types (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4) are circulating in Vietnam. Types 1 and 2 are dominant, accounting for approximately 90% of cases. Significantly, type 3 reappeared from the end of 2024, after many years of not being detected.
 You may also like Surveillance data from the southern region in September 2026 showed that DENV-2 accounted for 69% and DENV-1 accounted for 27.5% of the samples in which the virus type was identified. Because there is no cross-immunity between the virus types, a person can contract dengue fever up to four times.
 According to Professor Nguyen Van Kinh, more than 90% of people infected with the Dengue virus show no clinical symptoms but can still become a source of transmission. In addition, climate change, urbanization, and the development of insecticide-resistant mosquitoes are making the disease more difficult to predict and control. 
 Professor Nguyen Van Kinh analyzes the risk of reinfection with dengue fever due to the co-circulating four types of dengue virus. He also noted that the disease typically progresses through a fever phase and a critical phase. Between the 3rd and 7th day of the illness, even when the fever subsides, complications can still occur. Therefore, patients should not be complacent when their fever goes down but should continue to monitor for warning signs and return for follow-up appointments as directed by their doctor.
 Currently, there is no specific treatment for dengue fever. Professor Nguyen Van Kinh believes that a combination of vaccination, mosquito and larva eradication, and timely treatment is necessary to reduce the number of cases and limit fatalities. Vaccination is one of the preventive measures that needs attention, combined with eliminating stagnant water sources, limiting mosquito breeding grounds, and strengthening communication to encourage people to proactively prevent the disease.
 You may also like Several new points in the draft dengue fever treatment plan. 
 According to Professor Nguyen Van Kinh, the draft guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Dengue fever in 2026 are based on the 2023 guidelines, updated with new recommendations from the World Health Organization and practical treatment experience in Vietnam. The draft focuses on updating treatment for severe cases and complications; integrating treatment guidelines for children and adults. It also adds bedside ultrasound techniques to assess shock, the risk of shock or recurrent shock, supporting doctors in deciding on appropriate fluid replacement. Regarding prevention, the draft recommends combining Dengue fever vaccination with epidemiological surveillance, prevention, and control of disease-transmitting mosquitoes.
